newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to unveil new economic package, stocks soar.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to unveil new economic package, stocks soar.

text.p: South Korea said on Monday it would unveil a new economic package this week, and sent share prices rocketing.
"Finance and Economic Minister Kang Kyong-shik will release major economic measures in a news conference at 3 p.m. (0600 GMT) on Thursday," said a ministry spokesman.
Kang was named new finance minister in a sweeping cabinet reshuffle earlier this month.
Anticipation of the government's measures to boost the economy fuelled broad-based buying on the stock market. The main index jumped 2.66 percent, or 17.07 points, to 658.90 at Monday's close.
"The underlying market sentiment is strong because of the looming government announcement," said broker Hong-Jong-hyun of Coryo Securities.
Blue chips were the major beneficiaries. South Korea's largest chipmaker Samsung Electronics rose 2,000 won to 55,000 and the nation's biggest steelmaker POSCO added 2,300 won to 43,000.

Analysts and brokers said the economic package was expected to include measures to stabilise high interest rates and the weakening local currency, and to revamp the real name financial system. But they expected no short-term remedy to the slowing economy.
Ministry officials declined to give details.
"Investors believe the package will contain an expansion of foreign stock ownership ceiling," said analyst Kim Wan-hee of Dongsuh Securities.
Choi Dong-chul of Ssangyong Securities said the government was likely to issue long-term bonds to help raise money to finance building infrastrcture.
Analyst Hwang Chang-joong of LG Securities said a sharp rise in share prices was due partly to hopes the government would expand the shareholding limit for foreign investors.
After the market closed, a finance ministry official said the government was considering expanding the ceiling to 25-26 percent this year, instead of an earlier planned rise to 23 percent.
Foreigners can now buy up to 20 percent in a single company listed on the local bourse.
Analysts said the move would attract foreign funds and slow the won's fall against the dollar.
The finance ministry official said the government would take into account "factors other than the stock market" when it decides on the expansion of the foreign shareholding limit.

With South Korea's current account deficit hitting records, the won, which closed at 880.00 to the dollar on Monday, has lost 11.97 percent of its value against the U.S, unit since the beginning of 1996.
